message.content:
Let \(a=d_5\) and \(b=d_6\). Since \(a,b\mid n=a^2+b^2\), we have
\[
a\mid b^2,\qquad b\mid a^2.
\]
Write \(a=gx,\ b=gy\) with \(\gcd(x,y)=1\), \(x<y\). Then \(x\mid g\) and \(y\mid g\), so \(g=xyh\). Hence
\[
a=x^2yh,\qquad b=xy^2h,\qquad n=x^2y^2h^2(x^2+y^2).
\]

Because \(a=d_5\), all proper divisors of \(a\) are among the four divisors of \(n\) below \(a\), so \(\tau(a)\le 5\). If \(x\ge2\), then \(a\) is divisible by \(p^2\) for some prime \(p\mid x\) and by a distinct prime \(q\mid y\), giving \(\tau(a)\ge 3\cdot2=6\), impossible. Thus \(x=1\).

So
\[
a=yh,\qquad b=y^2h=ya,\qquad n=a^2(1+y^2),
\]
with \(y\ge2\). Also \(b=d_6\) gives \(\tau(b)\le6\). Enumerating \(b\) with \(\tau(b)\le6\) and \(y^2\mid b\), the only viable forms are
\[
b=p^2q \quad\text{or}\quad b=pq^2
\]
with distinct primes \(p,q\). In the first case \(y=p\), \(a=pq\). Since \(b\) has exactly six divisors, all divisors of \(n\) up to \(b\) must be divisors of \(b\). Thus \(q>p\), and \(1+p^2<b\) must divide \(b\), forcing
\[
q=1+p^2.
\]
This is prime only for \(p=2\), giving \(q=5\). Then
\[
n=p^2q^2(1+p^2)=2^2\cdot5^2\cdot5=500.
\]
The second case similarly gives \(p=5,q=2\), again yielding \(n=500\).

Indeed, the divisors of \(500\) begin
\[
1,2,4,5,10,20,\dots
\]
so \(d_5=10,\ d_6=20\), and
\[
10^2+20^2=100+400=500.
\]

\[
\boxed{500}
\]
